title: Is Your Recruiting Engagement Working? Signs to Track (October 2026)
summary: Use these October 2026 benchmarks to judge whether your recruiting engagement is converting outreach into real hires.
body_markdown:
Figuring out if your recruiter is working isn’t something most hiring managers think about until the role has been open too long. But the[recruiting progress signals](https://www.dover.com/) worth tracking show up well before any hire is close, and they’re concrete enough that you don’t need to rely on a status call to know where things actually stand.


**TLDR:**


-


Track pipeline stage movement, beyond outreach volume; a recruiter can send hundreds of messages with no real progress.


-


By weeks two to three, healthy outreach response rates tend to fall between 20 and 40 percent for most roles.


-


A bottom-heavy applicant score distribution often signals a miscalibrated role brief, not poor sourcing.


-


Separate bottlenecks you own (slow feedback, limited interview availability) from ones the recruiter owns before raising concerns.


-


Some tools pair a shared ATS with fractional recruiters at an average cost per hire of around $4,800 (varies by role and recruiter), making pipeline visibility a live number instead of a status update.


## Activity vs. Progress: Why the Distinction Matters Early


Recruiters can look extremely busy without your search actually going anywhere. Emails get sent, calls get taken, job boards get posted to, and none of it necessarily means a qualified candidate is closer to your offer.


Activity is what a recruiter does. Progress is what moves a candidate through a structured pipeline toward a decision.


What you want to track are[recruiting metrics for startups](https://www.dover.com/blog/recruiting-metrics-for-startups) like sourcing reach, outreach response rates, pipeline stage movement, and interview conversion.


## The Right Window to Start Assessing


The first week is mostly setup: intake calls, role brief alignment, sourcing strategy, job board distribution. The two-to-three-week mark is different. By then, sourcing volume should be measurable, outreach should have produced response data, and candidates should be moving into early pipeline stages. If none of that is visible by week three, that’s a real signal, not a ramp-up artifact.


## Sourcing Volume and Outreach Reach as Baseline Signals


By week two, sourcing volume is the first concrete number you can look at. A recruiter actively working a role should have profiled and reached out to a meaningful candidate pool, typically several dozen targeted profiles for most roles, more for competitive technical searches where response rates run lower.


Volume alone doesn’t tell you much, though, and it’s one of the[common problems with recruiting metrics](https://www.dover.com/blog/common-problems-with-recruiting-metrics-how-to-avoid-them) . A recruiter can send 200 outreach messages and generate no real pipeline if the profiles are off-spec or the messaging is weak. What you want to see alongside raw outreach numbers is response rate and profile quality.


### What Healthy Outreach Signals Look Like


A few working benchmarks worth keeping in mind, which are rules of thumb that vary by role, seniority, and outreach channel instead of an industry standard:


-


Response rates on personalized outreach tend to fall between 20 and 40 percent for most roles. Senior and highly specialized positions often run lower, so context matters when you’re reading the number.


-


If response rates are below 10 percent by week two, that’s worth a direct question about whether the targeting or messaging needs adjustment.


## Pipeline Stage Movement as the Clearest Leading Indicator


Sourcing activity populates a pipeline. Stage movement tells you whether that pipeline is actually working.


This is where the infrastructure layer matters. When a fractional recruiter and the hiring team operate inside a shared ATS, stage movement is visible in real time, no status call required to know whether a candidate advanced or stalled. Without that shared system, the only window into progress is whatever the recruiter chooses to share, which typically means a weekly update that lags the actual pipeline by days. The evaluation framework in the sections below assumes you can see pipeline data directly; if you can’t, getting that visibility is the prerequisite before any of these signals are readable.


By week two or three, watch for candidates advancing from sourced to screened to recruiter-interviewed, using[conversion metrics in recruiting](https://www.indeed.com/hire/c/info/conversion-metrics-in-recruiting) as the yardstick. If candidates are stacking up in the sourced stage without moving forward, the bottleneck sits somewhere between initial contact and qualification.


### What a Stalled Pipeline Usually Signals


A static pipeline is not a data gap, and it’s a common recruitment process bottleneck worth[reducing early](https://www.dover.com/blog/how-to-reduce-recruitment-process-bottlenecks-for-startups) . Candidates accumulating in early stages typically point to one of a few causes:


-


Outreach is generating responses, but screening criteria are filtering too aggressively and cutting candidates who might have been worth a conversation.


-


The recruiter is waiting on your feedback before advancing anyone, and that dependency has gone unacknowledged.


-


Qualified candidates are declining to move forward, and no one has surfaced why yet.


## What Applicant Scoring Results Tell You About Role Clarity


Applicant scoring results are usually read as a ranking tool. They’re more useful as a diagnostic.


When AI scoring clusters most inbound candidates at the low end, the instinct is to blame sourcing quality. Sometimes that’s right. But a flat or bottom-heavy score distribution often points somewhere else: the criteria defined at the[intake meeting](https://eddy.com/hr-encyclopedia/intake-meeting/) don’t match what you actually want in a hire.


If your scoring model is weighting years of experience heavily but your real bar is depth in a specific technical domain, the model will filter aggressively and look like sourcing is failing when the brief is just miscalibrated. Scoring makes that gap visible early, before weeks of sourcing effort compound the problem.


-


If most scored candidates fall below 50 percent, ask whether the criteria are too narrow or weighted incorrectly for the actual role.


-


If high-scoring candidates are consistently getting rejected after a recruiter screen, the scoring model may be optimizing for the wrong signals.


-


A healthy distribution has candidates spread across the range, with a meaningful cluster in the middle and some at the top.


## Interview Scheduling Activity as a Conversion Checkpoint


By week three, you should be able to look at your interview activity and see real numbers: how many interviews have been booked, how many hours your team has spent in conversations, and which roles or recruiters are driving that volume. A recruiting engagement that’s working converts sourced candidates into scheduled interviews at a visible rate across the[stages of the recruitment funnel](https://www.personio.com/hr-lexicon/recruitment-funnel/) .


-


Are interviews distributed across the hiring team, or stacked on one person? Concentration usually signals a scheduling bottleneck, not a recruiting one.


-


Is the interview count growing week over week, or did it spike once and flatten? Consistent growth is what you want.


-


Are interviews happening across multiple candidates, or is the same candidate being advanced repeatedly while others stall?


Seeing counts and hours per recruiter or per job in one view tells you quickly whether the pipeline is converting or just accumulating.


## How to Spot a Bottleneck Before It Costs You Candidates


Bottlenecks are rarely where they appear to be. A pipeline that looks stalled at the recruiter-screen stage might actually be waiting on feedback you haven’t returned yet. A sourcing problem might be a compensation problem in disguise.


The useful frame: separate bottlenecks you own from ones the recruiting engagement owns.


Bottlenecks you likely own, which line up with[SHRM’s recruiting guidance](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/workplace/complete-guide-to-effective-recruiting) on timely candidate feedback and limited interview rounds:


-


Feedback on screened candidates taking more than 48 hours, which causes warm candidates to accept other offers while they wait


-


Interview availability so limited that scheduling extends timelines by a week or more per candidate


-


Compensation bands that fall below market, showing up as consistently low response rates or late-stage candidate drop-off


Bottlenecks the engagement owns:


-


Outreach generating no responses after two weeks, suggesting messaging or targeting needs adjustment


-


Candidates advancing to your team and then receiving no disposition, creating pipeline buildup with no resolution and the kind of silence[candidate experience research](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/candidate-experience-talent-board-research-candes) links to candidate frustration


-


Recruiter screens not happening within a few days of a candidate responding, losing momentum at the first conversion point


## What a Healthy Two-to-Three-Week Engineering Pipeline Looks Like


For a reasonably scoped engineering role, two to three weeks in typically shows 60 to 100 sourced profiles skewing toward passive candidates with relevant stack experience, and a 20 to 35 percent response rate. Lower response rates on highly specialized searches (Rust, embedded systems, ML infrastructure) should be flagged and explained.


## What a Healthy Two-to-Three-Week Go-To-Market Pipeline Looks Like


Response rates for sales and customer success roles often land between 30 and 50 percent by week two, with 80 to 120 profiles sourced and a meaningful portion being passive candidates who aren’t actively applying.


Metric Engineering (weeks 2 to 3) GTM (weeks 2 to 3)


Profiles sourced 60 to 100 80 to 120


Outreach response rate 20 to 35% (lower for specialized roles) 30 to 50%


Recruiter screens completed or scheduled 8 to 15 10 to 20


Candidates advanced to hiring manager 2 to 5 3 to 6


Common breakdown point Zero recruiter screens by week 3 High response rate but low screened-to-advanced conversion (<20%)


Where GTM pipelines tend to break is at the qualification step. A high response rate followed by low advancement usually points to compensation bands that look misaligned once candidates hear the full package, or a role definition vague enough that the recruiter is screening loosely and passing through candidates who won’t survive a hiring manager conversation. If your screened-to-advanced rate is below 20 percent by week three, ask whether the intake criteria were specific enough about scope, quota expectations, or target market, the kind of gap a[dedicated recruiter model](https://www.dover.com/blog/dedicated-vs-multi-recruiter-hiring-model) surfaces faster than a shared marketplace search. Candidates with relevant GTM experience assess fit quickly and drop out early when that picture is unclear.


## How to Have a Productive Check-In Conversation with Your Recruiter


Pull your pipeline data before the call, not during it. Knowing the sourcing volume, response rate, and stage distribution going in means you can ask specific questions instead of trading impressions.


Questions worth asking at the two-to-three-week mark, which are part of learning[how to manage your Dover recruiter](https://www.dover.com/blog/how-to-manage-dover-fractional-recruiters) :


-


Which sourced candidates have been screened, and what was the disposition on each?


-


Where are candidates stalling, and who owns the next action?


-


Has outreach response rate shifted week over week, and if not, is a messaging adjustment worth testing?


-


Are there candidates you’ve advanced who haven’t received feedback, and how long has that been sitting?


When raising concerns about candidate quality, anchor feedback to specific profiles. Saying “the last three candidates didn’t have enterprise sales experience, which was a hard requirement” gives the recruiter something concrete to recalibrate against. A vague “the quality feels off” rarely produces a useful adjustment.


The goal is recalibration, not reassurance.

## FAQs


### How do you tell if a recruiting engagement is actually working in the first two to three weeks, before any hire is made?


Look at four numbers: sourcing volume, outreach response rate, pipeline stage movement, and interview scheduling activity. By week two, a recruiter actively working a role should have reached 60 to 120 targeted profiles, generated a response rate above 20 percent, and moved at least some candidates from sourced to screened. If none of those numbers exist yet, the engagement is behind, not ramping.


### What does a healthy outreach response rate look like for an engineering search vs. a GTM search?


Engineering roles typically run 20 to 35 percent by week two, with lower numbers for specialized disciplines like Rust or ML infrastructure. GTM searches often run 30 to 50 percent, which can make a pipeline look stronger than it is if you only watch response volume and not the screened-to-advanced conversion that follows.


### Do I need an ATS before bringing in a fractional recruiter, or does the recruiter bring their own tools?


The engagement works most cleanly when both parties operate inside a shared ATS. When the recruiter uses a separate system, pipeline visibility depends entirely on communication cadence rather than live data. Some fractional recruiting services include a shared ATS as part of the engagement; if yours doesn’t, building that visibility layer before the search starts produces faster feedback loops.


## Final Thoughts on Tracking Recruiting Progress Before It Costs You Good Candidates


Most searches that drag on longer than expected have a readable bottleneck somewhere in weeks two or three. The[recruiting progress signals](https://www.dover.com/) covered here, sourcing volume, response rates, pipeline stage movement, and interview counts, tell you where things slowed and who owns the next action. Dover’s shared-system model makes those numbers visible from day one, so you can ask specific questions early and course-correct before good candidates move on. Getting specific about that question early is what separates a search that builds momentum from one that resets every few weeks.
